UNC3753 Used Vishing and Physical Intrusions in U.S. Data Theft Extortion Campaign

The Hacker News
2026-06-08 18 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a financially motivated data theft extortion campaign that has targeted dozens of organizations across professional, legal, and financial services in the U.S. between January and May 2026. The activity has been attributed by Google Mandiant and Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) to a threat actor dubbed UNC3753, which is also known as

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Quick Assist launched followed by remote interactive session (UNC3753 vishing pretext) · [LLM] Privnote[.]com self-destructing-note URL access from corporate endpoint · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender · Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] AnyDesk, Bomgar, SuperOps or Zoho Assist installer execution (UNC3753 RMM foothold) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound connection to UNC3753 (Luna Moth) infrastructure IPs · [LLM] Outbound mail to or domain lookup of business-data-leaks[.]com (UNC3753 extortion infrastructure) · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] WinSCP or Rclone exfiltration from end-user workstations · [LLM] USB mass-storage attached followed by bulk file copy (UNC3753 physical intrusion) · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Quick Assist launched followed by remote interactive session (UNC3753 vishing pretext) AIDelivery Medium
Detects users launching Microsoft Quick Assist (quickassist.exe) and then a remote-controlled session beginning shortly after — the UNC3753 pretext for IT-help-desk vishing. Article-specific because UNC3753 explicitly named Quick Assist alongside Zoom/Teams as the screen-share entry vector. Rationale: Article names Quick Assist explicitly as a vector. The binary is fairly rare in most enterprises (Teams/Zoom are more common), so plain execution is a hunt-grade pivot. Corroborated with CISA & Microsoft advisories on Storm-1811/Quick Assist abuse. Cross-checked against: • https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2024/05/15/threat-actors-misusing-quick-assist-in-social-engineering-attacks-leading-to-ransomware/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1219/
ATT&CKT1219 T1566.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate corporate IT desktop support sessions
  • End-user-initiated Microsoft support call (consumer)
  • Quick Assist used as documented MSP onboarding workflow
  • Auto-launched by RemoteAssistance Group Policy on managed laptops
  • Pre-shipped to certain OEM image builds
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("it-helpdesk","corp-support")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user had a recorded ticket with internal IT help desk in the 15 minutes prior. Pull AccountName, DeviceName, and ProcessCommandLine. Pivot to user's mailbox (EmailEvents) for invoice-themed pretexts in last 24h. 2) Contain: if no legitimate ticket, isolate the device via Defender (Isolate Machine), force-reset the user's credentials, revoke active sessions. Block quickassist.exe via AppLocker or WDAC on the user group if Quick Assist is not in your sanctioned remote-support stack. 3) Hunt: pivot on AccountName across DeviceProcessEvents for AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho installers in the same 24-hour window, and on DeviceNetworkEvents for the article's UNC3753 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "quickassist.exe" or InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "quickassist.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\quickassist.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith "\\quickassist.exe"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Microsoft Quick Assist Execution (UNC3753 Vishing Pretext)
id: 6f2a8b3c-1c7d-4f50-a47b-2a3df9b1a401
description: Detects launch of Microsoft Quick Assist (quickassist.exe), abused by UNC3753/Luna Moth/SRG to obtain remote-control screen-share sessions after vishing IT-helpdesk pretexts.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/unc3753-used-vishing-and-physical.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/08
tags:
  - attack.t1219
  - attack.t1566.004
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\quickassist.exe'
  condition: selection
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\quickassist.exe OR *\QuickAssist.exe OR *\QUICKASSIST.EXE)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\quickassist\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="quickassist.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="quickassist.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="quickassist.exe" OR Processes.parent_process_name="quickassist.exe" by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
AnyDesk, Bomgar, SuperOps or Zoho Assist installer execution (UNC3753 RMM foothold) AIInstallation Medium
Detects fresh installation or first-time execution of the specific RMM tools UNC3753 instructs vishing victims to install (AnyDesk, Bomgar, SuperOps RMM, Zoho Assist). High-value hunting pivot since the article names these four explicitly. Rationale: Article explicitly names these four RMM tools as the post-vishing foothold mechanism. None should be ubiquitous in an org with a single sanctioned RMM — flag the deviations. Cross-checked against: • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa24-156a • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1020/
ATT&CKT1219 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned MSP using one of the four named tools
  • Sales engineer demo of Zoho or SuperOps
  • End user installs AnyDesk personal edition for home support
  • IT testing alternative RMM during procurement evaluation
  • Vendor support session pre-arranged via ticket
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !contains "\\Program Files\\<SanctionedRMMVendor>\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: cross-check against your sanctioned RMM allowlist. Pull AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, parent process. Check the user's mail for invoice-themed pretexts and call records / Teams call logs in the prior 60 minutes. 2) Contain: kill the RMM process tree, uninstall, force credential reset, revoke MFA tokens, block the RMM domains at the proxy if unsanctioned. 3) Hunt: pivot on the host for outbound to any of the article IPs (192.236.147.131, 192.236.147.138, 193.141.60.212, 192.236.154.158, 192.236.146.173, 174.169.162.62, 64.94.84.97), WinSCP/Rclone usage, and access to highly sensitive folder paths ("tax", "audit", "SSN", "client").
let RMMBinaries = dynamic(["anydesk.exe","bomgar-scc.exe","bomgarportal.exe","bomgar.exe","superops.rmm.agent.exe","superops_agent.exe","zohoassist.exe","zohomeeting.exe","za_connect.exe"]);
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ (RMMBinaries)
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("AnyDesk","Bomgar","SuperOps","Zoho Assist")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
let RMMBinaries = dynamic(["anydesk.exe","bomgar-scc.exe","bomgarportal.exe","bomgar.exe","superops.rmm.agent.exe","superops_agent.exe","zohoassist.exe","zohomeeting.exe","za_connect.exe"]);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ProcessFile = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,"\\")[-1]))
| where ProcessFile in (RMMBinaries)
   or CommandLine has_any ("AnyDesk","Bomgar","SuperOps","Zoho Assist")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Privnote[.]com self-destructing-note URL access from corporate endpoint AIDelivery Medium
Detects users browsing to privnote.com — the legitimate self-destruct-note service UNC3753 uses to deliver RMM install instructions during vishing calls without leaving recoverable evidence. Article-specific: privnote was explicitly named as the delivery channel. Rationale: Privnote is a legitimate but rarely-business-justified service. Article calls it out as UNC3753's instruction-delivery mechanism — DNS / proxy visibility on it is a cheap, high-signal pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://krebsonsecurity.com/2023/05/phishing-domains-tanked-after-meta-sued-freenom/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1102/
ATT&CKT1102 T1566.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Journalist / lawyer using privnote for legitimate confidential comms
  • User receives a privnote link from a known counterparty
  • Security researcher pivoting on threat-intel report
  • Personal use during break — non-work browsing
  • HR forwarding a sensitive doc one-time
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the user, time of access, and any process that subsequently spawned (RMM installer? PowerShell? cmd?) within 30 minutes. Ask the user directly — privnote use is uncommon. 2) Contain: if user reports an unsolicited helpdesk call, isolate device, reset creds, revoke sessions. 3) Hunt: 7-day org-wide privnote.com lookups to find peer victims; pivot any matching host on RMM execution and outbound to the UNC3753 IP set.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl has "privnote.com"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msmpeng.exe","mssense.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DnsQuery has "privnote.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName, EventVendor, EventProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Outbound connection to UNC3753 (Luna Moth) infrastructure IPs AICommand & Control Medium
Detects any endpoint or network egress to the seven IPs Mandiant/GTIG tied to UNC3753 (192.236.147.131, 192.236.147.138, 193.141.60.212, 192.236.154.158, 192.236.146.173, 174.169.162.62, 64.94.84.97). High-confidence alerting tier since these are specific IOCs. Rationale: Seven specific IOCs from the article — second-source corroborated against Mandiant/GTIG attribution to UNC3753 and FBI advisory. Direct-IP detections are high fidelity and low FP. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1020/ • https://www.ic3.gov/Media/News/2024/240712.pdf
ATT&CKT1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Network
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel researcher sandbox testing IOCs
  • Honeypot or red-team simulating UNC3753
  • Penetration test engagement using same IP range
  • Legitimate co-tenant on shared hosting provider (192.236.0.0/16 is ColoCrossing)
  • Crowd-sourced threat feed false-positive ingest
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sandbox.exe","cuckoo.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the source host, user, and process making the connection (InitiatingProcessFileName). Determine session length and byte counts — short HTTPS probes vs sustained file uploads tell very different stories. 2) Contain: isolate the host via Defender, block the IP at perimeter (firewall + EDR network containment), reset user creds & revoke MFA. 3) Hunt: 30-day lookback across the org on the same IP set; pivot on any host that hit it for WinSCP/Rclone exfil, Quick Assist/AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho Assist execution, and access to sensitive folder paths.
let UNC3753_IPs = dynamic(["192.236.147.131","192.236.147.138","193.141.60.212","192.236.154.158","192.236.146.173","174.169.162.62","64.94.84.97"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (UNC3753_IPs)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl
| order by Timestamp desc
let UNC3753_IPs = dynamic(["192.236.147.131","192.236.147.138","193.141.60.212","192.236.154.158","192.236.146.173","174.169.162.62","64.94.84.97"]);
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DstIpAddr in (UNC3753_IPs)
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkProtocol, EventVendor, EventProduct, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WinSCP or Rclone exfiltration from end-user workstations AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects WinSCP and Rclone process execution from user-context endpoints — UNC3753's named exfiltration tooling for staged sensitive data. Filters out IT-admin and backup-team baseline use. Rationale: Article names WinSCP and Rclone as the staged-exfil tooling. Both binaries are extremely rare in finance/legal services user contexts. Strong hunt-grade signal when scoped away from backup/IT. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1040/ • https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/cybersecurity-advisories/aa23-061a
ATT&CKT1567 T1048
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DevOps engineer pushing files to staging SFTP
  • Backup admin orchestrating cloud snapshots
  • Security team red-team data-exfil simulation
  • Database admin transferring schemas between regions
  • Developer using rclone with personal Google Drive remote
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("backupsvc","sftpsvc","devops") or DeviceName has_any ("backup","jumpbox","bastion","ci-runner"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the executing user has any documented business reason for WinSCP/Rclone (DevOps role? backup duties?). Pull full CommandLine — look for SFTP/FTPS/S3/GDrive remotes and the source path ("Documents", "Client", "Tax", "Audit"). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, block outbound on suspected destination, reset user creds and revoke sessions. Preserve volumes for forensics — extortion follow-up email may land within 30 minutes. 3) Hunt: pivot user/host for prior Quick Assist/AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho Assist execution, sensitive-folder enumeration (large numbers of file reads under client/tax/audit paths), and outbound to UNC3753 IP set.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("winscp.exe","winscp.com","rclone.exe")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("rclone copy","rclone sync","rclone copyto","winscp.com /command","open sftp://","open ftps://")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where not (InitiatingProcessAccountName has_any ("backupsvc","sftpsvc"))
| where not (DeviceName has_any ("backup","jumpbox","bastion"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| extend ProcessFile = tolower(tostring(split(NewProcessName,"\\")[-1]))
| where ProcessFile in ("winscp.exe","winscp.com","rclone.exe")
   or CommandLine has_any ("rclone copy","rclone sync","rclone copyto","winscp.com /command","open sftp://","open ftps://")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where not (SubjectUserName has_any ("backupsvc","sftpsvc"))
| where not (Computer has_any ("backup","jumpbox","bastion"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, AccountName=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, ParentProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

USB mass-storage attached followed by bulk file copy (UNC3753 physical intrusion) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects USB mass-storage attach events followed within 30 minutes by a high volume of file writes/reads against the device — modelling the FBI-reported UNC3753 escalation where threat actors enter offices in person posing as IT technicians and exfiltrate via external USB drives. Rationale: FBI advisory and the article both call out the new in-person USB-exfil escalation. Removable-media + bulk-write correlation on the user's workstation is the only telemetry surface for this physical-intrusion variant. Image [1] (vishing.jpg) reinforces the broader social-engineering pivot. Cross-checked against: • https://www.ic3.gov/Media/News/2024/240712.pdf • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1052/001/
ATT&CKT1052.001 T1200
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Employee transferring large dataset to encrypted corporate USB
  • Executive copying presentation deck to USB before travel
  • Field engineer offloading sensor data from removable disk
  • Marketing team archiving event photos to portable SSD
  • IT asset transfer / device retirement workflow
Suppression filter
| where AccountName !in~ ("backupsvc","itsupport")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the user account was physically on-site at attach time (badge logs, camera). Pull the AdditionalFields blob for USB vendor/serial. Check the user's tickets/calendar for an authorised IT visit. 2) Contain: revoke active sessions, suspend the account pending interview, isolate the host, and disable USB mass-storage class via GPO for the affected device. Preserve the workstation image. 3) Hunt: pivot the USB vendor/serial across the org — same drive on multiple hosts indicates a roaming insider/attacker. Cross-check physical access logs for unfamiliar visitors and review camera footage covering the attach time window.
let USBAttach = DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("UsbDriveMounted","PnpDeviceConnected","UsbDriveDriveLetterChanged")
    | project AttachTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, AdditionalFields;
let BulkCopy = DeviceFileEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
    | where FolderPath matches regex @"^[D-Z]:\\"
    | summarize FileCount = count(), FirstWrite=min(Timestamp), LastWrite=max(Timestamp), SampleFile=any(FolderPath) by DeviceId, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
    | where FileCount > 50;
USBAttach
| join kind=inner BulkCopy on DeviceId
| where FirstWrite between (AttachTime .. AttachTime + 30m)
| project AttachTime, FirstWrite, LastWrite, DeviceName, AccountName, FileCount, SampleFile, AdditionalFields
| order by AttachTime desc
let USBAttach = Event
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventLog == "Microsoft-Windows-DriverFrameworks-UserMode/Operational"
       or (EventLog == "System" and EventID in (20001,20003))
    | project AttachTime=TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID;
let BulkCopy = SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4663
    | where ObjectName matches regex @"^[D-Z]:\\"
    | summarize FileCount = count(), FirstAccess=min(TimeGenerated), LastAccess=max(TimeGenerated), SampleFile=any(ObjectName) by Computer, AccountName=SubjectUserName
    | where FileCount > 50;
USBAttach
| join kind=inner BulkCopy on Computer
| where FirstAccess between (AttachTime .. AttachTime + 30m)
| project AttachTime, FirstAccess, LastAccess, Computer, AccountName, FileCount, SampleFile
| order by AttachTime desc
source:windows.security @EventID:6416 @ClassName:DiskDrive
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/^[D-Z]:\\\\/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName], function=count(as=FileCount))
| FileCount > 50
ENDPOINT

| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" AND Filesystem.file_path IN ("E:\\*","F:\\*","G:\\*","H:\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count > 50 AND firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.action="created" AND Filesystem.file_path IN ("E:\\*","F:\\*","G:\\*","H:\\*") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | where count > 50 AND firstTime > relative_time(now(), "-7d@d")
Outbound mail to or domain lookup of business-data-leaks[.]com (UNC3753 extortion infrastructure) AICommand & Control High
Detects communications with business-data-leaks.com — the UNC3753 / Luna Moth data-leak-site domain referenced in extortion follow-ups. Any DNS lookup or email contact with this domain from the enterprise indicates either an in-progress extortion or a curious researcher. Rationale: Domain explicitly referenced in the article (LEAKEDDATA leak site) and corroborated by Mandiant attribution. Hits should be near-zero in normal enterprise traffic. Image [2] (LEAKEDDATA.png) corroborates the leak-site branding. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/groups/G1020/ • https://www.ic3.gov/Media/News/2024/240712.pdf
ATT&CKT1567 T1657
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Email.All_Email
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst pivoting on indicators
  • Legal team reviewing leak-site exposure of own client data
  • Sandbox detonation of a sample referencing the domain
  • CTI feed pre-fetching domain metadata
  • DLP scanner accessing dark/clear-web monitoring tool
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify whether the source is an end-user host (likely breach) or threat-intel pivot host (expected). Pull DNS / web logs and any inbound email from the domain. Search mailbox for extortion-style language ("three-day deadline", "data breach", "published"). 2) Contain: if end-user origin — declare incident, engage IR/legal/privacy, force credential reset across exposed user accounts, isolate originating host, preserve mailbox. 3) Hunt: 90-day org-wide lookup for the domain; pivot to UNC3753 IPs, WinSCP/Rclone runs, AnyDesk/Bomgar/SuperOps/Zoho Assist installations, and Quick Assist sessions to scope the incident.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where RemoteUrl has "business-data-leaks.com" | project Timestamp, DeviceName, Source="DeviceNetworkEvents", InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP),
(EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(30d) | where SenderFromAddress has "business-data-leaks.com" or SenderMailFromDomain has "business-data-leaks.com" | project Timestamp, DeviceName="", Source="EmailEvents", InitiatingProcessAccountName=RecipientEmailAddress, InitiatingProcessFileName=Subject, RemoteUrl=SenderFromAddress, RemoteIP="")
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where DnsQuery has "business-data-leaks.com" | project TimeGenerated, Source="DNS", SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, Indicator=DnsQuery),
(OfficeActivity | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d) | where Operation has_any ("Send","MailItemsAccessed") | where tostring(EventData) has "business-data-leaks.com" | project TimeGenerated, Source="Office365", SrcHostname="", SrcIpAddr=ClientIP, SrcUsername=UserId, Indicator="business-data-leaks.com")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```

    from datamodel=Web

     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)

    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Microsoft Teams external-tenant chat from unverified IT-helpdesk impersonator Delivery High
External Teams chat where displayName contains 'helpdesk' or 'IT support' — common 2024+ vishing pattern (Storm-1811, Black Basta, UNC6692). No CIM data model maps to Teams chats; uses raw O365 audit logs.
ATT&CKT1566.004 T1566
Data sourcesCloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where Application == "Microsoft Teams"
| where ActionType == "MessageSent"
| where RawEventData has "ExternalParticipants"
| extend SenderDisplayName = tostring(parse_json(RawEventData).SenderDisplayName)
| where SenderDisplayName matches regex @"(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)"
| project Timestamp, AccountDisplayName, IPAddress, ActivityType, SenderDisplayName, RawEventData
// External Teams chat — Teams audit lives in OfficeActivity.
OfficeActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OfficeWorkload == "MicrosoftTeams"
| where Operation in~ ("MessageSent","ChatCreated","TeamsImpersonationDetected")
| where isnotempty(UserId)
| where Subject has_any ("IT","helpdesk","support","password","verify")
   or Recipients has_any ("IT","helpdesk")
| project TimeGenerated, UserId, Operation, Subject, Recipients,
          ClientIP, UserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
CLOUD
`o365_management_activity`
  Workload=MicrosoftTeams Operation=MessageSent
  ExternalParticipants=*
| where match(SenderDisplayName, "(?i)(help.?desk|it.?support|service.?desk|tech.?support|admin)")
| stats count, earliest(_time) as firstTime, latest(_time) as lastTime
    by SenderUpn, SenderDisplayName, RecipientUpn, ChatId
RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard Installation High
ConnectWise / AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera installed outside IT change windows = common tradecraft for ransomware affiliates and IT-helpdesk impersonators.
ATT&CKT1219
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe")
   or FileName matches regex @"(?i)kaseya.*\.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\AnyDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\TeamViewer_Service.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\atera_agent.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\SplashtopStreamer.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\RustDesk.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\NinjaOne.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Remote-Management (RMM) Tool Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0c
status: experimental
description: |
    AnyDesk / TeamViewer / ScreenConnect / Atera / Splashtop /
    RustDesk — RMM tools attackers commonly install for hands-on-
    keyboard access. Filter against the IT estate's known tool.
references:

author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1219
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\AnyDesk.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("AnyDesk.exe","TeamViewer.exe","TeamViewer_Service.exe",
        "ScreenConnect.ClientService.exe","ConnectWiseControl.ClientService.exe",
        "atera_agent.exe","SplashtopStreamer.exe","RustDesk.exe","NinjaOne.exe","kaseya*.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental

logsource:
    category: process_access

            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'

ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:

        Image|endswith:
            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'
    selection_wmic_remote:
        Image|endswith:

level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
       OR (Processes.process_name="wmic.exe" AND Processes.process="*/node:*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'

        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'

falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Network connections to article IPs / domains Command & Control High
Outbound traffic to attacker infrastructure named in the article.

Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web Network_Resolution.DNS DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)

| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl,

let BadIPs     = dynamic(["192.236.147.131", "192.236.147.138", "193.141.60.212", "192.236.154.158", "192.236.146.173", "174.169.162.62", "64.94.84.97"]);

ImNetworkSession

title: Outbound Connection to Article-Named IP / Domain
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d0f
status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__IP_LIST__` / `__DOMAIN_LIST__` placeholders with
    article-specific destinations. For dynamic IOC management, use a
    watchlist or external feed.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/tactics/TA0011/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.command-and-control
logsource:
    category: network_connection
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_ip:
        DestinationIp:
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__IP_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    selection_domain:
        DestinationHostname:
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_1__'
            - '__DOMAIN_PLACEHOLDER_2__'
    condition: selection_ip or selection_domain
falsepositives:
    - None on a true-positive IOC match
level: critical
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("192.236.147.131", "192.236.147.138", "193.141.60.212", "192.236.154.158", "192.236.146.173", "174.169.162.62", "64.94.84.97")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("business-data-leaks.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("business-data-leaks.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer
     | `drop_dm_object_name(DNS)`]
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.dest IN ("192.236.147.131", "192.236.147.138", "193.141.60.212", "192.236.154.158", "192.236.146.173", "174.169.162.62", "64.94.84.97")
    by All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest, All_Traffic.dest_port
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Web
        where Web.dest IN ("business-data-leaks.com")
        by Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`]
| append
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS
        where DNS.query IN ("business-data-leaks.com")
        by DNS.src, DNS.query, DNS.answer

| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or SHA1 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce") or MD5 in~ ("52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["52fda5c1b9704544f32ee98d9060e689", "51d39aa39478beeac94f2d12f682ecce"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Bright Data SDK control-plane beacon to proxyjs/clientsdk endpoints AICommand & Control High
Detects DNS or TLS SNI resolution to the Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control channels (proxyjs/clientsdk on bright-sdk.com, brdtnet.com, luminatinet.com). Any endpoint resolving these is either running an app embedding brdsdk.framework or actively relaying scraping jobs as an exit node. Rationale: All five FQDNs (proxyjs.brdtnet.com, proxyjs.luminatinet.com, proxyjs.bright-sdk.com, clientsdk.bright-sdk.com, clientsdk.brdtnet.com) are explicitly named in the article body and corroborated by the Include Security research blog as the SDK's exclusive control-plane channel — the article itself recommends blocking them at the router. The article also notes Bright Data's paid commercial service runs on different hosts, so hits here are specifically the embedded-SDK exit-node behaviour. Cross-checked against the Include Security research blog (https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/) which added the broader *.luminati.io SNI pattern and the brdsdk.framework binary identifier. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Data-engineering team running a sanctioned Bright Data paid scraper proof-of-concept and pointing it at the shared SDN endpoints
  • Security researcher VM (e.g. malware sandbox, threat-intel analyst) intentionally executing a partner app to reproduce the Include Security teardown
  • DNS resolver / threat-intel feed cache pre-resolving newly-published IOCs without an actual user-driven query
  • Corporate guest WiFi hosting employee BYOD smart-TV streaming sticks or phones that have a Bright Data partner app installed
  • Vendor or supplier remote-access laptops where users installed Petflix-style free consumer apps off-hours
Suppression filter
// Suppress sanctioned Bright Data paid-service test hosts (uncomment and populate)
// | where DeviceName !in~ ("scraping-poc-01","data-eng-vm-bd")
// Suppress sandbox/researcher subnets
// | where ipv4_is_in_any_range(RemoteIP, dynamic(["10.99.0.0/24"])) == false
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the resolving asset from Defender DeviceInfo / DHCP — is it a corp endpoint, a managed iPhone, a smart TV on guest VLAN, or unknown IoT? Confirm InitiatingProcessFileName on Defender hits (iOS will surface the host app bundle ID; corp Windows hitting these is unusual and a separate concern). 2) Contain: Sinkhole all five FQDNs and the *.bright-sdk.com / *.brdtnet.com / *.luminatinet.com / *.luminati.io suffixes at the corporate DNS resolver and egress firewall; if the asset is a corp-issued iPhone, push an Intune compliance check that blocks the offending host app. 3) Hunt: Pivot on the source IP across the last 30 days of NetFlow / proxy logs for sustained high-fan-out HTTPS egress (UC3 logic); query DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory and Intune app inventory for any other devices reporting the same partner-app bundle so you can scope the affected fleet.
// Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control-plane beacon
// Endpoints contacting *.bright-sdk.com / *.brdtnet.com / *.luminatinet.com
let brdControlHosts = dynamic(["proxyjs.brdtnet.com","proxyjs.luminatinet.com","proxyjs.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.brdtnet.com"]);
let brdSuffixes = dynamic([".bright-sdk.com",".brdtnet.com",".luminatinet.com",".luminati.io"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (brdControlHosts)
    or RemoteUrl has_any (brdSuffixes)
| extend MatchType = case(RemoteUrl in~ (brdControlHosts), "control-plane FQDN",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".bright-sdk.com", "bright-sdk.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".brdtnet.com", "brdtnet.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".luminatinet.com", "luminatinet.com suffix",
                          RemoteUrl endswith ".luminati.io", "luminati.io suffix",
                          "other")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, DeviceId, InitiatingProcessAccountName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, MatchType
| order by Timestamp desc
// Bright Data residential-proxy SDK control-plane beacon — ASIM DNS view
let brdControlHosts = dynamic(["proxyjs.brdtnet.com","proxyjs.luminatinet.com","proxyjs.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.bright-sdk.com","clientsdk.brdtnet.com"]);
let brdSuffixes = dynamic([".bright-sdk.com",".brdtnet.com",".luminatinet.com",".luminati.io"]);
(union isfuzzy=true
  (ImDnsActivity
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where DnsQuery in~ (brdControlHosts)
       or DnsQuery has_any (brdSuffixes)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Indicator = DnsQuery, Source = "ImDnsActivity"),
  (CommonSecurityLog
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where isnotempty(DestinationHostName)
   | where DestinationHostName in~ (brdControlHosts)
       or DestinationHostName has_any (brdSuffixes)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = SourceIP, SrcHostname = SourceHostName, SrcUsername = SourceUserName,
             Indicator = DestinationHostName, Source = strcat(DeviceVendor,"/",DeviceProduct)),
  (DnsEvents
   | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
   | where Name has_any (brdSuffixes) or Name in~ (brdControlHosts)
   | project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr = ClientIP, SrcHostname = Computer, SrcUsername = "", Indicator = Name, Source = "DnsEvents"))
| summarize FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Hits = count(),
            Indicators = make_set(Indicator, 25), Sources = make_set(Source, 5)
            by SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname
| order by LastSeen desc

Bright Data partner-app or brdsdk.framework present on managed iOS / mobile inventory AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the managed mobile/endpoint fleet for installed apps that ship the Bright Data residential-proxy SDK (brdsdk.framework v1.532.120) — using the article-named partner-app list (Petflix, PlayWorks Digital, CloudTV, Longvision) and Bright Data's published partner page. Catches the exit-node *at install time* rather than waiting for it to phone home. Rationale: Article explicitly names Petflix (Roku), PlayWorks Digital, CloudTV, and Longvision as Bright Data partners shipping the SDK, and identifies brdsdk.framework v1.532.120 as the binary. Include Security additionally surfaced the Swift symbols BrdWebSocketFacade and BrdNetwork.DNSResolver inside the framework. Article notes the partner list is not 1:1 with current SDK inclusion (each app must be verified independently), so this is a hunt not an alert. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1195.001 T1474.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Software
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Security research team intentionally side-loaded the partner app on a managed device to reproduce the teardown
  • Employee BYOD device enrolled in MDM with a legitimately-installed free TV/streaming app where the developer has since removed the SDK
  • Partner-app vendor whitelisted by Procurement for a specific business use case (e.g. a marketing team approved CloudTV for an ad campaign monitor)
  • Generic name collision — "PlayWorks" or "CloudTV" could match unrelated apps; verify the bundle ID against Bright Data's published partner page
  • Inventory delay — an app uninstalled hours ago may still show in DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory until the next sync
Suppression filter
// Exclude approved BD test devices (populate with your scraping-POC fleet)
// | where DeviceName !in~ ("sec-research-ios-01","sec-research-ios-02")
Response runbook
1) Triage: Pull the exact bundle ID / package name from DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory and cross-check against Bright Data's public partner page; eliminate name-collision FPs. Confirm whether the device has actually beaconed to the UC1 control-plane domains within 14 days. 2) Contain: Add the confirmed bundle IDs to the Intune / MDM compromised-app list and force-uninstall on managed devices; for BYOD, push a compliance policy that blocks corporate resource access until the app is removed. 3) Hunt: Pivot DeviceImageLoadEvents on any device for the brdsdk.framework load event or the Swift symbols BrdWebSocketFacade / BrdNetwork.DNSResolver to find apps not on the published partner list that nonetheless embed the SDK.
// Hunt managed fleet for Bright Data SDK partner apps and the brdsdk.framework binary
let brdPartnerApps = dynamic(["Petflix","PlayWorks","CloudTV","Longvision"]);
let brdVendors = dynamic(["PlayWorks Digital","CloudTV","Longvision","Bright Data","Luminati"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any (brdPartnerApps)
    or SoftwareVendor has_any (brdVendors)
    or SoftwareName contains "brdsdk"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, DeviceType, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, DeviceType, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers, EndOfSupportStatus
| union (
    DeviceImageLoadEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where FileName contains "brdsdk" or FolderPath contains "brdsdk.framework" or FileName has_any ("BrdWebSocketFacade","BrdNetwork")
    | project DeviceId, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
  )
| order by DeviceName asc
// Hunt managed fleet (Defender via Sentinel + Intune) for Bright Data SDK partner apps
let brdPartnerApps = dynamic(["Petflix","PlayWorks","CloudTV","Longvision"]);
let brdVendors = dynamic(["PlayWorks Digital","CloudTV","Longvision","Bright Data","Luminati"]);
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareName has_any (brdPartnerApps)
    or SoftwareVendor has_any (brdVendors)
    or SoftwareName contains "brdsdk"
| join kind=leftouter (DeviceInfo | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, OSPlatform, DeviceType, PublicIP) by DeviceId) on DeviceId
| project DeviceId, DeviceName, OSPlatform, DeviceType, SoftwareVendor, SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion, PublicIP

Smart-TV / mobile device acting as residential proxy exit node (high-fan-out HTTPS to unrelated public destinations) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts firewall and NetFlow telemetry for the behavioural signature of a Bright Data exit node: a single internal source (typically an unmanaged smart TV or mobile device) initiates a high volume of outbound HTTPS sessions to many unrelated public web destinations the user is not actively browsing, often during off-hours. The 200 GB/month SDK cap and the device's always-on TV / mobile profile shape the threshold. Rationale: Article quantifies the SDK's monthly traffic ceiling (200 GB/mo, uncapped in some regions) and notes the device 'keeps relaying in the background while someone is watching the screen or on a call, as long as the battery is not low'. The behavioural fingerprint — single internal source, hundreds of unrelated public destinations per hour, outbound bytes ≈ inbound bytes (proxy relay, not browsing) — is what survives even if Bright Data rotates control-plane domains. Article warns 'Bright Data could also change how the SDK connects in the future, which would mean any blocklist needs updating' which is exactly why a behavioural UC complements UC1's IOC UC. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.includesecurity.com/2026/06/the-smart-tv-in-your-livingroom-is-a-node-in-the-aiscraping-economy/
ATT&CKT1090.002 T1496 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Corporate VPN concentrator or split-tunnel egress gateway — many destinations, high volume, but the source IP is a known infrastructure host
  • Marketing / SEO crawler or competitive-intelligence scraping VM the business legitimately runs
  • Backup appliance or DR replication target uploading to many regional cloud endpoints
  • Smart-home hub (e.g. Home Assistant, Hubitat) polling dozens of cloud APIs concurrently from an IoT VLAN
  • Update server / mirror replicating from many upstream package repositories during a patch window
Suppression filter
// Exclude known infrastructure egress points (VPN concentrators, web crawlers, backup targets)
// | where SourceIP !in ("10.10.5.20","10.10.5.21","10.20.1.0/24")
// Exclude SEO/marketing crawlers
// | where SourceHostName !startswith "crawl-"
Response runbook
1) Triage: Map SourceIP to asset via DHCP, NAC, or DeviceInfo — is it a managed endpoint, a known infrastructure host (VPN/proxy/crawler), or unattributed IoT/guest? Pull a 24h destination-host sample and look for residential-proxy tells: unrelated industries, geographic spread, e-commerce/news/forum mix, no clear business affinity. 2) Contain: If asset is unmanaged smart TV or guest-network device, quarantine VLAN port and apply the UC1 sinkhole; if it's a managed iPhone, push Intune block on the offending host app and confirm via UC2 inventory. 3) Hunt: Cross-correlate SourceIP with UC1 hits in the prior 14 days; check whether the same MAC/asset has historically resolved any *.bright-sdk.com / *.brdtnet.com / *.luminatinet.com; pull NetFlow byte-out trend for the device for the prior 30 days to confirm sustained 200GB/month pacing.
// Managed iOS / mobile exhibiting residential-proxy egress pattern (covers Defender for iOS estate)
let WindowHrs = 1h;
let MinUniqueRemoteIPs = 100;   // residential browsing rarely fans out to >100 distinct public IPs per hour
let MinSessions = 500;          // SDK polling + scraping job throughput floor
let ManagedMobile = DeviceInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(24h)
    | where OSPlatform in ("iOS","iPadOS","Android")
    | summarize arg_max(Timestamp, OSPlatform, DeviceType, PublicIP, LoggedOnUsers) by DeviceId, DeviceName;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(24h)
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| join kind=inner ManagedMobile on DeviceId
| summarize UniqueRemoteIPs = dcount(RemoteIP),
            UniqueRemoteUrls = dcount(RemoteUrl),
            Sessions = count(),
            SampleUrls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 25),
            SampleProcess = make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName, 10),
            FirstSeen = min(Timestamp),
            LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, DeviceId, OSPlatform, bin(Timestamp, WindowHrs)
| where UniqueRemoteIPs > MinUniqueRemoteIPs and Sessions > MinSessions
| extend MultiUseSig = iff(UniqueRemoteUrls > 200 and array_length(SampleProcess) <= 2, "likely-proxy", "review")
| order by Sessions desc
// Residential-proxy exit-node behavioural hunt against firewall logs
// Surfaces internal sources fan-out HTTPS to many unrelated public destinations (Bright Data exit-node signature)
let WindowHrs = 1h;
let MinUniqueDests = 250;       // home/IoT devices very rarely exceed this per hour
let MinBytesOut = 524288000;    // 500 MB outbound per hour (200 GB/mo SDK cap → ~280 MB/hr avg, peaks higher)
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(24h)
| where DeviceVendor in ("Palo Alto Networks","Fortinet","Cisco","Check Point","Zscaler","SonicWall")
| where DestinationPort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and isnotempty(DestinationIP)
| where ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP) == false
| summarize UniqueDestHosts = dcount(DestinationHostName),
            UniqueDestIPs = dcount(DestinationIP),
            BytesOut = sum(toint(SentBytes)),
            BytesIn = sum(toint(ReceivedBytes)),
            Sessions = count(),
            SampleHosts = make_set(DestinationHostName, 25)
            by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, WindowHrs)
| where UniqueDestHosts > MinUniqueDests and BytesOut > MinBytesOut
| extend GbOut = round(BytesOut / 1073741824.0, 2)
| extend EgressInboundRatio = round(BytesOut * 1.0 / (BytesIn + 1), 2)
| where EgressInboundRatio > 0.4   // proxy traffic: outbound ~= inbound, unlike normal browsing which is inbound-heavy
| order by BytesOut desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=true 
    dc(All_Traffic.dest) as uniqueDests 
    dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as uniqueDstIPs 
    sum(All_Traffic.bytes_out) as bytesOut 
    sum(All_Traffic.bytes_in) as bytesIn 
    count as connCount

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic 
    where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (80,443) AND All_Traffic.action=allowed 
    by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_category _time span=1h
| `drop_dm_object_name("All_Traffic")`
| where uniqueDests > 250 AND bytesOut > 524288000
| eval gbOut = round(bytesOut/1073741824, 2)
| where src_category IN ("iot","smart_tv","mobile","unknown","guest")
| sort - bytesOut

    dc(All_Traffic.dest) as uniqueDests 
    dc(All_Traffic.dest_ip) as uniqueDstIPs

    sum(All_Traffic.bytes_in) as bytesIn

    from datamodel=Network_Traffic 
    where All_Traffic.dest_port IN (80,443) AND All_Traffic.action=allowed 
    by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_category _time span=1h
