Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] GHOST STADIUM FIFA lookalike domain resolution (fifa.bio/.center/.gold/.red/.sale/.shopping/.show/.ski) · [LLM] GHOST STADIUM PingIdentity SSO clone: external referrer hot-linking fifa.com static assets · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Massiv / Perseus (Cerberus-derived) Android banking trojan APK hash on managed endpoint · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] GHOST STADIUM phishing kit / Android trojan C2 IP egress (8 specific hosts) · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
GHOST STADIUM FIFA lookalike domain resolution (fifa.bio/.center/.gold/.red/.sale/.shopping/.show/.ski) AIDelivery High
Detects DNS resolution or HTTP connection from corporate or employee endpoints to the specific FIFA World Cup 2026 lookalike domains attributed to GHOST STADIUM. Hits indicate a user followed a Facebook ad, Telegram/WhatsApp link or SEO result into the cloned PingIdentity SSO phishing kit. Rationale: Domain list is the exact GHOST STADIUM cluster registered since August 2025 (per Group-IB tracking cited in the article). These are not legitimate FIFA properties — fifa.com is the only legitimate root — so any internal endpoint resolving them is high-fidelity initial-access signal. Cross-checked against the kill-chain Phase 1 IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fifa-world-cup-2026-scams-are-already.html
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1583.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat researchers / TI analysts manually validating the IOCs from their workstation
  • Sandbox detonation traffic mirrored into production telemetry
  • Security awareness platforms running simulated-phishing campaigns reusing the same domains
  • DNS sinkhole responders pointing the domains at internal honeypots
  • Employees who are genuine ticket-seeking fans visiting them on personal device traversing corporate Wi-Fi
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe") or not (DeviceName has_any ("sandbox","sec-research","malware-analyst","detonation"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the user, device and any browser process that issued the resolution. Pivot to web proxy for the same source IP within ±5 minutes — was a POST issued to the domain (credential submission)? Check Defender UrlClickEvents / SafeLinks for the referring email or Teams/Slack message. Step 2 (contain): Block the eight domains plus the GHOST STADIUM C2 IPs at proxy/DNS/firewall. If credentials were entered, force-reset the user's password, revoke active sessions, and treat their FIFA SSO and Microsoft 365 SSO as compromised. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep 30 days of DNS for any other registrar variant (fifa.* TLD permutations newly observed), correlate hits to Vidar/LummaC2/RedLine stealer-log feeds, and pivot device→APK installs to surface any Massiv/Perseus payload on the same employee's mobile.

| extend HostPart = tolower(tostring(parse_url(RemoteUrl).Host))
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| where HostPart in (GhostStadiumDomains) or HostPart endswith ".fifa.bio" or HostPart endswith ".fifa.center" or HostPart endswith ".fifa.gold" or HostPart endswith ".fifa.red" or HostPart endswith ".fifa.sale" or HostPart endswith ".fifa.shopping" or HostPart endswith ".fifa.show" or HostPart endswith ".fifa.ski"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, HostPart

let GhostStadiumDomains = dynamic(["fifa.bio","fifa.center","fifa.gold","fifa.red","fifa.sale","fifa.shopping","fifa.show","fifa.ski"]);

GHOST STADIUM phishing kit / Android trojan C2 IP egress (8 specific hosts) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects outbound connections from any internal endpoint (workstation, mobile via NAT, server) to the eight IP addresses that host the cloned fifa.com phishing infrastructure and serve as C2 for the Massiv/Perseus Android banking trojans. Article-specific IP set, not a reputation feed. Rationale: These are the exact infrastructure IPs Group-IB enumerated for the GHOST STADIUM cluster cited in the article. Eight discrete /32 destinations — small enough to enumerate, large enough to span the cloned-site fleet and the trojan C2. Any internal-to-IP connection is high-signal because none of these IPs front legitimate enterprise services. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fifa-world-cup-2026-scams-are-already.html
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1437.001 T1583.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Shared-hosting collateral — other unrelated sites on the same IP if it's a multi-tenant VPS
  • Outbound sandbox / malware-detonation appliance routing through corporate egress
  • Threat intel platforms (URLscan, VirusTotal scanner workers) doing active probes against the IOCs
  • Penetration-testing or red-team engagements re-using the same IPs as targets
  • Bring-your-own mobile devices on guest Wi-Fi forwarding through corporate NAT
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !has_any ("sandbox","sec-research","detonation","redteam")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Map source IP→device→user via DHCP/Defender DeviceInfo. Identify the initiating process (mobile = mostly browser; desktop = browser or sideload helper). Pull the 10-minute window before the connection to find the inducing click (fifa.* domain, Telegram/WhatsApp URL, Facebook ad redirect). Step 2 (contain): Block the eight IPs at perimeter firewall and on EDR network containment; if a corporate-managed Android device is implicated, MDM-wipe it — Massiv/Perseus accessibility takeover cannot be cleanly evicted otherwise. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep 30 days for the same eight IPs across all telemetry, correlate to fifa.* DNS hits, search Vidar/LummaC2/RedLine stealer-feed dumps for the affected user's corporate UPN and FIFA SSO email, and pull any APK file writes matching the three SHA1s from any download channel.
let GhostStadiumC2 = dynamic(["148.178.18.23","148.178.18.60","154.86.0.33","207.56.1.93","66.112.212.25","148.178.16.48","148.178.16.5","104.225.235.49"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteIP in (GhostStadiumC2)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","ConnectionAttempt","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, Protocol
| order by Timestamp desc
let GhostStadiumC2 = dynamic(["148.178.18.23","148.178.18.60","154.86.0.33","207.56.1.93","66.112.212.25","148.178.16.48","148.178.16.5","104.225.235.49"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog

Massiv / Perseus (Cerberus-derived) Android banking trojan APK hash on managed endpoint AIInstallation Medium
Detects the three specific SHA1 hashes of the trojanised RojaDirecta-style streaming APKs distributed alongside the World Cup 2026 fraud campaign. Matches against any file-write or download channel (browser saves, MDM-relayed install records, USB transfers) where the bytes touch a corporate-managed device. Rationale: These three SHA1 hashes are explicitly named in the kill-chain Phase 2 IOCs as the Massiv/Perseus APKs. SHA1 collisions across legitimate software are vanishingly rare; the APK extension + streaming-themed filename adds defense in depth for catching repacks even if the exact hash drifts. Highest-confidence host-side signal in the campaign. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fifa-world-cup-2026-scams-are-already.html
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1660 T1626.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Mobile-threat researchers storing the samples on their workstations for analysis
  • EDR signature pack containing the hash as a payload (the hash literal appears in a YARA/IOC file, not the malware itself)
  • Corporate email security gateway extracting and quarantining the APK as an attachment
  • DFIR forensic copies of an already-compromised device's storage
  • Sandbox detonation artefacts pulled back into corporate file shares
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","SenseIR.exe") and DeviceName !has_any ("sec-research","sandbox","malware-analyst","dfir-")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Identify host, user and source of the file (FileOriginUrl tells you the download source; cross-reference with the eight GHOST STADIUM IPs and fifa.* domains). If the host is a Windows desktop, the APK is almost certainly destined for a personal Android via cable / cloud sync — pivot to the user's enrolled mobile. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file, isolate the host. If the file appeared on a managed Android device, MDM-wipe immediately — Perseus reads notes/banking/authenticator apps and harvests OTPs, so credential rotation is required, not optional. Reset the user's banking and corporate SSO passwords, revoke MFA tokens, and treat any SMS-OTP-protected account as already breached. Step 3 (hunt): Search the prior 30 days for any other APK with the same FileOriginUrl, sweep DeviceNetworkEvents for the eight GHOST STADIUM C2 IPs from the user's devices, and check whether their corporate credentials appear in any Vidar/LummaC2/RedLine stealer-feed delivery received du
let MassivPerseusHashes = dynamic(["3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1","84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c","9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA1 in (MassivPerseusHashes) or (FileName endswith ".apk" and (FileName has_any ("roja","directa","fifa","worldcup","stream","futbol","soccer")))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA1, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, FileOriginReferrerUrl, FileOriginIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let MassivPerseusHashes = dynamic(["3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1","84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c","9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileSHA1 in (MassivPerseusHashes)
   or (TargetFileExtension =~ "apk" and TargetFileName has_any ("roja","directa","fifa","worldcup","stream","futbol","soccer"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA1, TargetFileSHA256

GHOST STADIUM PingIdentity SSO clone: external referrer hot-linking fifa.com static assets AIDelivery Medium
Detects the signature visual-evasion technique of the GHOST STADIUM phishing kit — the cloned login page hot-links images directly from fifa.com so that brand-similarity scanners see the assets as legitimate. Hunts for outbound requests to fifa.com static-asset paths whose Referer header is NOT a fifa.com hostname. Rationale: The article explicitly describes this evasion: "It loads its images straight from FIFA's own servers, so the page looks authentic and slips past tools that flag copied images." Hot-linking inverts the normal Referer relationship — a phishing page loads fifa.com/<asset> with its own non-fifa hostname in the Referer header. Whitelisting fifa.com itself, PingIdentity (the real SSO provider), and search engines isolates the phishing-kit traffic shape. This is the rare detection that catches the kit's structural choice, not just the rotating IOC list. Cross-checked against: • https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fifa-world-cup-2026-scams-are-already.html
ATT&CKT1656 T1036.005 T1608.005
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate news / blog articles embedding fifa.com images via direct <img src=fifa.com/...> tags
  • Web archive (archive.org / archive.today) snapshots being viewed by employees
  • Translation proxies (Google Translate) rewriting fifa.com pages and preserving asset hot-links
  • Social media link-preview cards (Slack/Teams/Twitter unfurl bots) fetching og:image
  • Browser extensions that inline-display fifa.com content (e.g. RSS readers, news aggregators) with their own host in Referer
Suppression filter
| where ReferrerHost !endswith ".archive.org" and ReferrerHost !endswith ".archive.today" and ReferrerHost !startswith "translate." and ReferrerHost !endswith ".slack-edge.com" and not (HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent has_any ("Slackbot","Twitterbot","facebookexternalhit","LinkedInBot"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): For each hit, examine the ReferrerHost — that is the candidate phishing site. WebFetch the URL from a sandboxed analyst VM and compare visually to fifa.com. If a PingIdentity-style login form is rendered, treat as confirmed clone. Pivot to the user's browser history within ±5 minutes for any POST to the referrer or to a non-fifa.com URL with login form data. Step 2 (contain): Submit the phishing URL to Microsoft / Google Safe Browsing, block the host across proxy/DNS/firewall, and add it to the org's URL deny-list. If the user submitted credentials, force a global password reset, revoke active SSO sessions, and treat any reused FIFA SSO credential against corporate accounts as breached. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot the ReferrerHost to the eight GHOST STADIUM C2 IPs (resolve and check passive DNS); enumerate all other employees who hit the same ReferrerHost in the last 30 days; sweep for fifa-themed inbound emails containing the host in URLs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess","HttpConnectionInspected")
| where isnotempty(RemoteUrl)
| extend RemoteUrlLower = tolower(RemoteUrl)
| where RemoteUrlLower has "fifa.com"
| where RemoteUrlLower matches regex @"fifa\.com/.+\.(jpg|jpeg|png|svg|webp|gif|css)(\?|$)"
   or RemoteUrlLower has_any ("fifa.com/assets/","fifa.com/static/","fifa.com/images/","fifa.com/_next/")
| join kind=inner (
    DeviceEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
    | where ActionType == "BrowserLaunchedToOpenUrl" or AdditionalFields has "Referrer"
    | extend Referrer = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).Referrer)
    | where isnotempty(Referrer) and Referrer !contains "fifa.com" and Referrer !contains "pingidentity.com"
    | project DeviceId, RefTime=Timestamp, Referrer
  ) on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (RefTime .. RefTime + 30s)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, Referrer, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP
| order by Timestamp desc
let LegitimateReferrers = dynamic(["fifa.com","www.fifa.com","pingidentity.com","ping.fifa.com","fifa.tm","ticketing.fifa.com"]);
ImWebSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where Url matches regex @"(?i)fifa\.com/.+\.(jpg|jpeg|png|svg|webp|gif|css)(\?|$)"
   or Url has_any ("fifa.com/assets/","fifa.com/static/","fifa.com/images/","fifa.com/_next/")
| extend ReferrerHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(HttpRequestHeaderReferer).Host))
| where isnotempty(HttpRequestHeaderReferer)
| where not (ReferrerHost in (LegitimateReferrers))
| where not (ReferrerHost endswith ".fifa.com")
| where ReferrerHost !has "google." and ReferrerHost !has "bing." and ReferrerHost !has "duckduckgo."
| project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, SrcUsername, ReferrerHost, Url, HttpRequestHeaderReferer, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent
| order by TimeGenerated desc
@http.url:(*fifa.com/assets/* OR *fifa.com/static/* OR *fifa.com/images/* OR *fifa.com/_next/* OR *fifa.com/*.jpg OR *fifa.com/*.png OR *fifa.com/*.svg) -@http.referrer:(*fifa.com* OR *pingidentity.com* OR *google.* OR *bing.*) -@http.referer:(*fifa.com* OR *pingidentity.com* OR *google.* OR *bing.*)

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.

Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or SHA1 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or MD5 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or SHA1 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a") or MD5 in~ ("3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["3b8bb7631b39f455d31544b55ba97b49ab1888c1", "84ecdca915f1af822ccc8a04479f5179104f353c", "9bd164dd3f50d196c7dff4f6c1b0f1345ac96d9a"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

PCPJack Hijacks 230 AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure Servers for Covert SMTP Relay Network

The Hacker News
2026-06-05 14 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

The threat actor known as PCPJack has hijacked cloud servers associated with Amazon Web Services (AWS), Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure to create a covert SMTP email relay network. "Compromised business servers across the U.S., Europe, and Asia were quietly converted into SMTP proxies, verified for mail relay capability, and synced to a downstream consumer every five minutes," Hunt.io said in

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] PCPJack exit-IP enrichment lookups to api.ipify.org and ip-api.com from Linux workloads
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — PCPJack Hijacks 230 AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure Servers for Covert SMTP Relay N
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] PCPJack hidden Chisel implant drop at /var/tmp/.xs on Linux
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Outbound C2 to PCPJack Sliver server 213.136.80.73 (esp. port 9000) · [LLM] PCPJack SOCKS5 listener bound to deterministic port 10000-14999 on Linux · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PCPJack SMTP quality-gate probe to smtp.gmail.com:587 from non-mail Linux workloads · [LLM] SCP exfiltration of PCPJack proxy lists to downstream collector 38.242.204.245 · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Outbound C2 to PCPJack Sliver server 213.136.80.73 (esp. port 9000) AICommand & Control Medium
Detect any host beaconing to the PCPJack Sliver C2 IP 213.136.80.73 — particularly the port 9000 health-check the diagnostic script polls and the SCP/SSH (22) and HTTPS callbacks beacons use. Highest-confidence indicator in the article: the C2 IP itself was confirmed open and live by Hunt.io. Rationale: 213.136.80.73 is the unauthenticated PCPJack C2 server Hunt.io confirmed live with ports 8444/9443/9000 exposed; pivoting on the IP alone is high-fidelity. Cross-checked Hunt.io's write-up and the prior SentinelOne PCPJack analysis. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel • https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/cloud-worm-evicts-teampcp-and-steals-credentials-at-scale/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel sandbox or detonation system intentionally connecting to the IOC
  • TI-feed enrichment service performing reputation lookups against the IP
  • Security researcher hunting tools mapping the C2 from a known SOC subnet
  • Tor exit-node operator whose node happens to relay through this IP (rare)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("defender-sandbox.exe","detonator.exe") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\ThreatIntel\\")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify host, process and user; pull process tree (Sliver implant typically dropped at /var/tmp/.xs on Linux) and check for Chisel binaries on disk. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host via EDR, block 213.136.80.73 and 38.242.204.245 egress at perimeter, snapshot for forensics. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound traffic for SOCKS5 listener ports 10000-14999, SCP to 38.242.204.245, SMTP probes to smtp.gmail.com:587, and persistence (cron/systemd) referencing /var/tmp/.xs.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP == "213.136.80.73"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Protocol, ActionType, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| extend Port9000Health = iif(RemotePort == 9000, "yes", "no")
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP == "213.136.80.73"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstIP=DestinationIP, DstPort=DestinationPort, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "213.136.80.73"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstIP=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetProto=NetworkProtocol, EventVendor, EventProduct, DvcAction)
| extend Port9000Health = iif(DstPort == 9000, "yes", "no")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

id: 7e3c5a0d-5d11-4b6c-9a32-3a8b9d1d4f01
description: Network connection to the PCPJack Sliver C2 IP (Hunt.io, June 2026). The actor uses this host for Sliver beacon check-in and exposes a port 9000 health probe consumed by the diagnostic script.
references:

  - attack.t1571

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:213.136.80.73) OR (source:linux.auditd @network.destination.ip:213.136.80.73) OR (source:cloudtrail @network.client.ip:213.136.80.73)
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6)
| RemoteAddressIP4="213.136.80.73" OR RemoteAddressIP6="213.136.80.73"

NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.src) as src values(All_Traffic.src_ip) as src_ip values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as dest_port values(All_Traffic.transport) as transport values(All_Traffic.app) as app from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="213.136.80.73" by All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port host | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | eval is_port9000=if(dest_port==9000,1,0) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

PCPJack SMTP quality-gate probe to smtp.gmail.com:587 from non-mail Linux workloads AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunt for the Sliver deployer's outbound 'mail relay capability' probe to smtp.gmail.com:587, which the script uses to filter beacons worth keeping. A cloud VM (AWS/GCP/Azure) opening port 587 to gmail from a non-mail workload is a sharp PCPJack-specific signal. Rationale: The article's SMTP quality gate is literally a TCP 587 probe to smtp.gmail.com — extremely specific behaviour for a non-mail workload. Confirmed by Hunt.io's primary source. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1090 T1071
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate mail relay or transactional-mail VM (Postfix/Sendmail) actually configured to send via Gmail
  • Application-tier code using Gmail SMTP for password-reset or notification email
  • DevOps test of newly-built golden image's outbound mail capability
  • Backup/monitoring agent sending alert email via personal Gmail
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["mailrelay01","mailrelay02","smtp-egress-01"])) and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (dynamic(["postfix","sendmail","opendkim","msmtp","exim4"]))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm whether the source host is a sanctioned mail relay (check IPAM/CMDB). If not, capture full process tree — the initiating process should be the Sliver implant at /var/tmp/.xs or a Chisel binary. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, block egress to 213.136.80.73 and 38.242.204.245, suspend cloud instance credentials. Step 3 — Hunt: search same host for the deployer script artefacts (cron entry, systemd unit referencing /var/tmp/.xs), port-9000 callbacks to C2, and any SCP traffic to 38.242.204.245.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemotePort == 587
| where RemoteUrl =~ "smtp.gmail.com" or RemoteUrl endswith ".gmail.com"
| where DeviceName !in~ (dynamic(["mailrelay01","mailrelay02"]))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DestinationPort == 587
  | where DestinationHostName has "smtp.gmail.com" or DestinationDnsDomain has "gmail.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstHost=DestinationHostName, DstIP=DestinationIP, DstPort=DestinationPort, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DstPortNumber == 587
  | where DstHostname has "smtp.gmail.com" or DstDomain has "gmail.com"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstHost=DstHostname, DstIP=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol, NetProto=NetworkProtocol)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PCPJack SMTP relay capability probe to smtp.gmail.com:587
id: 1c8a0e92-4f15-4d7b-8a44-c1c3e7b2a902
description: Outbound SMTP submission (587) to smtp.gmail.com from a workload — used by the PCPJack Sliver deployer as a quality gate to decide whether a beacon is worth keeping for the relay pipeline.
references:

  - https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
author: SOC Detection Engineering

(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationPort:587 @DestinationHostname:*smtp.gmail.com*) OR (source:linux.auditd @network.destination.port:587 @network.destination.ip:(64.233.184.108 OR 64.233.184.109 OR 142.250.0.0\/15)) OR (source:cloudtrail @evt.name:AuthorizeSecurityGroupEgress @requestParameters.ipPermissions.items.toPort:587)
(#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 OR #event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP6)
| RemotePort=587

SCP exfiltration of PCPJack proxy lists to downstream collector 38.242.204.245 AIActions on Objectives High
PCPJack syncs the verified-proxy list every five minutes via SCP to 38.242.204.245. Hunt for SSH/SCP/rsync connections to this IP, or process events showing scp/sftp invoking this destination on Linux beacons. Rationale: 38.242.204.245 is the named downstream collector receiving five-minute SCP syncs; pairing the IP with scp/rsync command-line keeps FP low. Confirmed by Hunt.io. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1041 T1567
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate ops team using 38.x ranges for backup destinations (very rare for this specific IP)
  • SOC researcher actively probing the IOC from a known investigative host
  • Threat-intel pipeline pulling the IP for indicator enrichment
  • Backup job whose configuration is misconfigured to a typo'd destination
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/lib/backup/" and AccountName !in~ ("backupsvc","veeamsvc")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the source host is not a sanctioned backup origin; capture full scp/rsync command line and the parent process. Expect the parent to be the Sliver implant or a deployer script. Step 2 — Contain: isolate host, rotate SSH keys present on the host, block 38.242.204.245 at perimeter, snapshot for forensics. Step 3 — Hunt: extract the SSH known_hosts / authorized_keys, search for /var/tmp/.xs persistence, hunt across the fleet for any other host that has scp'd to the same collector.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteIP == "38.242.204.245"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemotePort, ActionType),
(DeviceProcessEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where FileName in~ ("scp","sftp","rsync","sshpass","ssh")
  | where ProcessCommandLine has "38.242.204.245"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationIP == "38.242.204.245"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SourceHostName, SrcIP=SourceIP, DstIP=DestinationIP, DstPort=DestinationPort, AppProto=ApplicationProtocol),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DstIpAddr == "38.242.204.245"
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHost=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, DstIP=DstIpAddr, DstPort=DstPortNumber, AppProto=NetworkApplicationProtocol),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where ActingProcessName has_any ("scp","sftp","rsync","sshpass")
  | where ActingProcessCommandLine has "38.242.204.245"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName)
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SCP/rsync to PCPJack downstream collector 38.242.204.245
id: 6f1d2e74-3c20-4a8e-9c9b-d0d2b6c1f203
description: SCP, SFTP or rsync targeting 38.242.204.245 — the PCPJack downstream that receives the verified-proxy list every five minutes (Hunt.io, June 2026).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/pcpjack-hijacks-230-aws-google-cloud.html
  - https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/05
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1041
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: linux
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith:
      - '/scp'
      - '/sftp'
      - '/rsync'
  selection_dst:
    CommandLine|contains: '38.242.204.245'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_dst
level: high
(source:linux.auditd @auditd.type:EXECVE @process.name:(scp OR sftp OR rsync OR sshpass) @process.command_line:*38.242.204.245*) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @DestinationIp:38.242.204.245) OR (source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @CommandLine:*38.242.204.245*)
(#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\/(scp|sftp|rsync|sshpass)$/i CommandLine=/38\.242\.204\.245/) OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemoteAddressIP4="38.242.204.245")
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
NETWORK

| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Processes.user) as user values(Processes.process) as cmd from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("scp","sftp","rsync","sshpass") OR Processes.process="*scp*38.242.204.245*" OR Processes.process="*rsync*38.242.204.245*") by Processes.dest Processes.process_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | append [ | tstats summariesonly=t count from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_ip="38.242.204.245" by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.dest_ip All_Traffic.dest_port | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` ] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)

PCPJack hidden Chisel implant drop at /var/tmp/.xs on Linux AIInstallation High
On the victim side the Sliver/Chisel binary is dropped as the hidden dot-prefixed file /var/tmp/.xs. Detect creation of this exact path, or any executable written to /var/tmp/ whose name starts with '.', then chmod'd +x. Rationale: /var/tmp/.xs is an exact path called out in the article as the persistence location for the Sliver/Chisel binary. Filtering well-known dot dirs keeps FPs minimal. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1564.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate user creating .swp/.swo Vim swap files in /var/tmp (mostly excluded by extension)
  • systemd-tmpfiles pruning sweeping in dot-prefixed lockfiles
  • Build pipeline using /var/tmp/.cache or /var/tmp/.npm style scratch directories
  • Sanctioned admin debug script dropping a dotfile for troubleshooting
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("vim","vi","nvim","systemd-tmpfiles") and not (FileName endswith ".swp" or FileName endswith ".swo")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull SHA256 of the dropped file and hash-check against VT/internal TI; identify the parent process and user that created the file. Step 2 — Contain: kill the implant process, quarantine the binary, isolate the host, rotate credentials present on the host, revoke cloud-instance IAM role session if compromised. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate cron and systemd persistence referencing /var/tmp/.xs, check for Chisel tunnel listeners on 10000-14999, and check fleet for the same file path and hash.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/"
| where FileName startswith "." and FileName !in~ (".X11-unix",".ICE-unix",".font-unix")
| extend IsXs = iif(FolderPath == "/var/tmp/.xs" or FileName == ".xs", "yes", "no")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, IsXs
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType in ("FileCreated","FileModified","FileCreate")
| where TargetFilePath startswith "/var/tmp/"
| where TargetFileName startswith "." and TargetFileName !in~ (".X11-unix",".ICE-unix",".font-unix")
| extend IsXs = iif(TargetFilePath == "/var/tmp/.xs" or TargetFileName == ".xs", "yes", "no")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, IsXs
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: PCPJack Chisel implant dropped as /var/tmp/.xs

PCPJack SOCKS5 listener bound to deterministic port 10000-14999 on Linux AICommand & Control Medium
The deployer derives each beacon's SOCKS5 proxy port from an MD5 of its Sliver UUID, mapped to 10000-14999. Hunt for newly-bound listeners in that port range on Linux servers, especially when the listener is a non-standard binary in /var/tmp or /tmp. Rationale: The 10000-14999 SOCKS5 port range is explicitly called out and derived from MD5(UUID); restricting to listeners spawned from /var/tmp or /tmp narrows it to PCPJack-likely cases. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1090.001 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Application servers using ephemeral high ports for legitimate microservices
  • Kubernetes NodePort services that fall in the 10000-14999 band
  • Developer running a local web server / proxy out of /tmp during testing
  • Monitoring agent that opens a transient debug port from /tmp
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/usr/lib/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/opt/" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith "/snap/"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the listening process binary path and hash; confirm it's not part of an approved app inventory. Look for sibling Chisel binaries on the host. Step 2 — Contain: kill the listener, isolate the host, block 213.136.80.73 and 38.242.204.245 egress. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the binary's hash across the fleet, examine cron/systemd persistence, look for the chisel_verifier.py-style 60-second cycle of port probes from C2.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("ListeningConnectionCreated","InboundConnectionAccepted")
| where LocalPort between (10000 .. 14999)
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFileName startswith "."
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, LocalIP, LocalPort, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where NetworkDirection in ("Inbound","Listen")
| where SrcPortNumber between (10000 .. 14999) or DstPortNumber between (10000 .. 14999)
| extend Port = coalesce(SrcPortNumber, DstPortNumber)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), DistinctPorts=dcount(Port), PortList=make_set(Port,50), Connections=count() by DvcHostname, EventVendor, EventProduct
| where DistinctPorts >= 1
| order by FirstSeen desc
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:3 @SourcePort:[10000 TO 14999]) OR (source:linux.auditd @network.client.port:[10000 TO 14999] @process.executable.path:(\/var\/tmp\/* OR \/tmp\/.*))
#event_simpleName=NetworkListenIP4 LocalPort>=10000 LocalPort<=14999
| ContextImageFileName=/\/(var\/)?tmp\//i OR ContextImageFileName=/\/\.[^\/]+$/
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, LocalPort], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app values(All_Traffic.src) as src from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_port>=10000 All_Traffic.src_port<=14999 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_port host | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats values(src_port) as ports dc(src_port) as port_count by src | where port_count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.app) as app values(All_Traffic.src) as src from datamodel=Network_Traffic where All_Traffic.src_port>=10000 All_Traffic.src_port<=14999 All_Traffic.transport=tcp by All_Traffic.src All_Traffic.src_port host | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)` | stats values(src_port) as ports dc(src_port) as port_count by src | where port_count>=1 | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
PCPJack exit-IP enrichment lookups to api.ipify.org and ip-api.com from Linux workloads AIReconnaissance Medium
After SMTP-gate verification PCPJack enriches each proxy with exit IP, country, and ASN via api.ipify.org and ip-api.com. Linux servers calling these enrichment services back-to-back (especially right after suspicious SMTP probing) are likely PCPJack-converted relays. Rationale: api.ipify.org and ip-api.com are named in the article as the enrichment path PCPJack uses to label proxies. Two distinct lookups from the same host is a strong PCPJack-shape signal. Cross-checked against: • https://hunt.io/blog/pcpjack-230-cloud-servers-smtp-proxy-network-sliver-chisel
ATT&CKT1016 T1590.005
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Geolocation library bundled with a SaaS app legitimately checking exit IP
  • CI runner verifying its outbound IP for IP-allowlist validation
  • Personal-use script (curl ifconfig.me) by an admin
  • VPN client checking effective public IP after dial-up
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ (dynamic(["curl","wget"])) or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: identify the process making the call and whether it lives in /var/tmp or /tmp; correlate with same-host SMTP probes to smtp.gmail.com:587. Step 2 — Contain: if the process is the PCPJack implant, kill it, quarantine /var/tmp/.xs, isolate the host. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the host's outbound to 213.136.80.73, SCP to 38.242.204.245, and Chisel listeners in 10000-14999.
let Enrichers = dynamic(["api.ipify.org","ip-api.com","ipinfo.io","ifconfig.me","icanhazip.com"]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteUrl in~ (Enrichers) or RemoteUrl has_any (Enrichers)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), HostsHit=make_set(RemoteUrl,10), Hits=count() by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| where array_length(HostsHit) >= 2 or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/var/tmp/" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath startswith "/tmp/"
| order by FirstSeen desc
let Enrichers = dynamic(["api.ipify.org","ip-api.com","ipinfo.io","ifconfig.me","icanhazip.com"]);
union isfuzzy=true
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where DnsQuery in~ (Enrichers) or DnsQuery has_any (Enrichers)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, Query=DnsQuery, EventVendor, EventProduct),
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
  | where HttpHostName in~ (Enrichers) or Url has_any (Enrichers)
  | project TimeGenerated, Host=SrcHostname, SrcIP=SrcIpAddr, Query=HttpHostName, Url, HttpMethod)
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Lookups=make_set(Query,10), Hits=count() by Host, SrcIP
| where array_length(Lookups) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688

Stata binary spawning OS shell (CVE-2026-47708 stata-mcp log_file_name injection) AIExploitation High
Detects the Stata executable (or its Linux/macOS variants) spawning cmd/powershell/sh/bash/python child processes. This is the direct exploitation signal for CVE-2026-47708, where an attacker injects Stata's `shell` command via the unsanitised log_file_name parameter on the MCP `stata_do` tool, breaking out of the `log using "..."` string to execute arbitrary OS commands. Rationale: The article states the injection breaks out of the Stata `log using "..."` string so that `shell <cmd>` is interpreted as a Stata command, which then spawns an OS shell. Stata processes (stata.exe, stata-mp.exe, stata-se.exe, stata-be.exe, xstata variants) legitimately almost never spawn cmd/powershell/sh/bash/python children, so the parent-child pivot from the article's exploitation primitive is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against the GHSA advisory body (GHSA-4p62-hqp5-g644) and the linked fix commit which confirms log_file_name was interpolated raw into the Stata command string. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4p62-hqp5-g644 • https://github.com/SepineTam/stata-mcp/commit/e6f945941ae0c7cf5e74a428e0b3dc82b396382f • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
ATT&CKT1059 T1190 T1059.003 T1059.004
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researcher do-files that legitimately call Stata's `shell` command to run git/make/system tooling
  • Stata's built-in `python` integration where researchers intentionally exit to a Python interpreter
  • Local development of stata-mcp itself where the developer is testing tool invocations
  • Stata batch wrappers (e.g. Stata-launch scripts via cmd.exe) where cmd.exe is briefly used to set environment before invoking stata — appears as stata→cmd in reverse direction (parent flip)
  • Defender ASR/EDR sensor self-test scripts that intentionally walk every parent-child combination
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("git ","make ","type ","dir ","ls -") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".do")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine of the child shell and the InitiatingProcessCommandLine of the Stata parent; check whether the Stata cmdline references a `.do` file path that came from an MCP / stata-mcp tool invocation, and whether the child shell command line contains data-exfil patterns (curl/wget/nc/Invoke-WebRequest, base64, /tmp/, /dev/tcp/). Confirm the installed `stata-mcp` pip package version on the host — anything <1.17.3 is vulnerable. Step 2 — Contain: if the shell child issued network/file actions, isolate the host via Defender machine action / EDR network-isolate; kill the parent Stata PID and the stata-mcp Python wrapper process; rotate any credentials the Stata process had filesystem access to. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the parent Stata PID's file writes (UC2 below) for `.log` files with shell metacharacters in the filename; pivot on the stata-mcp wrapper's parent (often python.exe / uvx / pipx) and search for inbound MCP requests carrying `log_file_name
DeviceProcessEvents

| where FileName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","sh.exe","zsh.exe","bash","sh","zsh","python.exe","python","python3")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256, InitiatingProcessParentFileName

Stata-authored log file written with shell metacharacters or path traversal in filename (CVE-2026-47708) AIExploitation High
Detects file writes by Stata or the stata-mcp Python wrapper where the target `.log` filename contains shell metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&`, backtick, single/double quotes) or path traversal (`..`). The article shows the PoC produces a literal log file whose filename contains the injected payload — even if the `shell` portion fails, the file artifact itself is a deterministic exploitation footprint. Rationale: The article's PoC explicitly shows the generated path becomes `<log_dir>/'; shell echo pwned > /tmp/pwned.txt; '.log` — i.e. the log filename literally contains a semicolon, single-quote, and redirection metacharacters, and (per `generate_log_file` having no path-traversal guard) may also contain `..`. Both observations come directly from the article's source-code excerpts and PoC. Filtering DeviceFileEvents to Stata/Python writers with `.log` extension narrows scope to near-zero baseline, and the regex on metacharacters/traversal isolates the exploitation artefact from any legitimate workflow. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-4p62-hqp5-g644 • https://github.com/SepineTam/stata-mcp/commit/e6f945941ae0c7cf5e74a428e0b3dc82b396382f
ATT&CKT1190 T1059 T1083
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Researchers using single-quote in legitimate log filenames (e.g. `obama'speech.log`) — uncommon
  • Stata batch runs where the dataset name embedded into the log filename happens to contain a hyphen-prefixed value that looks like `..` (e.g. `panel..2024.log`)
  • Test fixtures inside the stata-mcp source tree that exercise the (now-fixed) parsing path
  • CI runners that intentionally fuzz the log_file_name parameter post-patch as a regression test
  • Backup/sync tools (rsync, OneDrive) writing `.log` artefacts with versioned suffixes that include quote characters
Suppression filter
| where not (TargetFileName matches regex @"^panel\.\.20[0-9]{2}\.log$" or FolderPath has "\\stata-mcp\\tests\\fixtures\\")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: read the full TargetFileName and FolderPath; reconstruct the original `log_file_name` payload the attacker sent to the MCP `stata_do` tool. Pull all sibling file activity (especially writes to /tmp/, %TEMP%, or anywhere outside the configured Stata log_file_path) from the same InitiatingProcessId — path-traversal in the same payload often writes a second file at an arbitrary location. Check the host's installed stata-mcp version (`pip show stata-mcp`) — vulnerable is <1.17.3. Step 2 — Contain: kill the Stata + stata-mcp wrapper processes; quarantine the malformed .log file and any second-payload files for IR; restrict the MCP server's listener (typically a local HTTP/stdio endpoint) until upgraded to ≥1.17.3. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on InitiatingProcessId to find any child shells (UC1) and any outbound network connections within the next 60s; search the MCP server's request logs (if proxied) for `log_file_name` values containing quote/semicolon/newline characters; expand

Mini Shai-Hulud npm worm exfiltration to t.m-kosche.com OpenTelemetry endpoint AIActions on Objectives High
Detects DNS/HTTP egress to the TeamPCP exfiltration C2 at t.m-kosche.com, where stolen creds are POSTed to /api/public/otel/v1/traces masquerading as OpenTelemetry traffic. High-fidelity because the FQDN and URI path are unique to this campaign and corroborated by Wiz, Snyk and Socket. Rationale: Pivots on the exact exfil FQDN (t.m-kosche.com) and the unique OpenTelemetry-disguise URI path (/api/public/otel/v1/traces) called out in Wiz, Snyk and Socket write-ups of the same Mini Shai-Hulud / TeamPCP wave that published @cap-js/openapi@1.4.1 on 2026-05-19. Both strings are unambiguous IOCs with no benign collisions. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://socket.dev/blog/sap-cap-npm-packages-supply-chain-attack • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/monitoring-npm-supply-chain-attacks/ • https://thehackernews.com/2026/05/mini-shai-hulud-pushes-malicious-antv.html

Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: confirm the resolving/connecting process is node, npm, npx, yarn, pnpm or bun (not chrome/edge browsing the IOC article). Pull the parent process tree and the package.json directory walk back to identify which npm scope (@cap-js, @antv, @lint-md, etc.) preinstall fired. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host from network, kill node/bun, block t.m-kosche.com at proxy/DNS-firewall, immediately revoke ALL credentials reachable from that workstation (npm tokens, GitHub PATs, AWS/Azure/GCP keys, SSH private keys, kubeconfig, Vault tokens). Assume creds are already compromised — rotate, don't audit. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the host's npm registry mirror logs for `npm publish` calls (worm propagation), and on GitHub audit log for new public repos created by the developer's PAT in the last 14 days (backup exfil channel).
// Mini Shai-Hulud TeamPCP exfil endpoint
let exfilHost = "t.m-kosche.com";
let exfilPath = "/api/public/otel/v1/traces";
union isfuzzy=true
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where RemoteUrl has exfilHost or RemoteUrl has exfilPath
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
            Source="DeviceNetworkEvents"),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(30d)
  | where ActionType in ("DnsQueryResponse","ConnectionSuccess","NetworkConnectionEvents")
  | where RemoteUrl has exfilHost or AdditionalFields has exfilHost
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName,
            InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
            InitiatingProcessFolderPath, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort,
            Source="DeviceEvents")
| order by Timestamp desc
// Mini Shai-Hulud TeamPCP exfil endpoint - DNS + web egress
let exfilHost = "t.m-kosche.com";
let exfilPath = "/api/public/otel/v1/traces";
union isfuzzy=true
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Name has exfilHost
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType, Source="DnsEvents"),
(ImDnsActivity
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DnsQuery has exfilHost
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Name=DnsQuery, QueryType=DnsQueryTypeName, Source="ImDnsActivity"),
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where DestinationHostName has exfilHost or RequestURL has exfilPath or RequestURL has exfilHost
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=SourceHostName, ClientIP=SourceIP, Name=DestinationHostName, QueryType=RequestURL, Source="CommonSecurityLog"),
(ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where Url has exfilHost or Url has exfilPath
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, ClientIP=SrcIpAddr, Name=DstHostname, QueryType=Url, Source="ImWebSession")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mini Shai-Hulud TeamPCP npm Worm C2 Domain (t.m-kosche.com)
id: a1b2c3d4-e5f6-4789-abcd-1234567890ab
description: Detects DNS resolution or network connection to t.m-kosche.com, the TeamPCP / Mini Shai-Hulud npm-worm exfiltration endpoint disguised as OpenTelemetry trace ingest.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jpvj-wpmj-h7rv
  - https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm
  - https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1041
  - attack.t1567
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName|endswith:
      - 't.m-kosche.com'
      - '.m-kosche.com'
  condition: selection
falsepositives:
  - Security analyst manually resolving IOC during triage
  - DNS sinkhole logging
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:22 AND @QueryName:(*t.m-kosche.com* OR *T.M-KOSCHE.COM*)) OR (source:windows.sysmon AND @EventID:3 AND @DestinationHostname:(*t.m-kosche.com* OR *T.M-KOSCHE.COM*)) OR (source:(linux.auditd OR linux.syslog) AND @network.destination.domain:*m-kosche.com*) OR @http.url:*t.m-kosche.com/api/public/otel/v1/traces*
(#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/(^|\.)m-kosche\.com$/i) OR (#event_simpleName=NetworkConnectIP4 RemotePort=443) | (DomainName=/(^|\.)m-kosche\.com$/i OR (in(field=RemoteAddressIP4))) | groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, DomainName, RemoteAddressIP4], function=[count(), min(@timestamp), max(@timestamp)]) | sort(_count, order=desc)
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.src) as src values(DNS.dest) as dns_server from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*t.m-kosche.com*" by DNS.query DNS.src | `drop_dm_object_name("DNS")` | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.src) as src values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as port from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_hostname="*t.m-kosche.com*" OR All_Traffic.url="*t.m-kosche.com*" by All_Traffic.dest_hostname All_Traffic.url] | append [| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.src) as src from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*t.m-kosche.com*" OR Web.url="*/api/public/otel/v1/traces*" by Web.url Web.user] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(DNS.src) as src values(DNS.dest) as dns_server from datamodel=Network_Resolution.DNS where DNS.query="*t.m-kosche.com*" by DNS.query DNS.src | `drop_dm_object_name("DNS")` | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(All_Traffic.src) as src values(All_Traffic.dest_port) as port from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic where All_Traffic.dest_hostname="*t.m-kosche.com*" OR All_Traffic.url="*t.m-kosche.com*" by All_Traffic.dest_hostname All_Traffic.url] | append [| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime values(Web.src) as src from datamodel=Web where Web.url="*t.m-kosche.com*" OR Web.url="*/api/public/otel/v1/traces*" by Web.url Web.user] | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Bun runtime spawned by npm/node preinstall hook (TeamPCP setup.mjs loader) AIInstallation High
Detects the Mini Shai-Hulud execution chain where the compromised npm preinstall hook in @cap-js/openapi (and sibling packages) invokes the Bun JavaScript runtime to load setup.mjs → execution.js. Bun is rarely a child of npm/node in enterprise environments and is the campaign's signature loader. Rationale: Wiz and Socket both document the bun-runtime loader chain (preinstall→setup.mjs→bun→execution.js) as the Mini Shai-Hulud signature. Bun being spawned by npm/node is rare outside dedicated Bun shops, and pairing it with the `preinstall` / `setup.mjs` / `execution.js` strings caught in cmdline lifts confidence dramatically. Cross-checked against: • https://www.wiz.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-supply-chain-sap-npm • https://socket.dev/blog/sap-cap-npm-packages-supply-chain-attack • https://snyk.io/blog/mini-shai-hulud-antv-npm-supply-chain-attack/ • https://safedep.io/mini-shai-hulud-strikes-again-314-npm-packages-compromised/
ATT&CKT1195.002 T1059.007 T1546.016
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer monorepo that uses Bun as a faster install/test runner and shells out from npm-orchestrated scripts
  • CI pipeline that intentionally runs `npm test` → `bun run` for performance
  • Bun installer itself (`bun install`) running during initial dev-environment setup, parented by node bootstrap
  • Vendor SDK that bundles a Bun-based build step (e.g., some Tauri/Bun hybrid projects)
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "bun install" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","WindowsTerminal.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bash.exe","zsh") and ProcessCommandLine !has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js"))
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture the full process tree (bun's grandparent should be the originating npm/yarn/pnpm install command); pull the working directory and search it for node_modules/@cap-js/openapi/package.json containing version 1.4.1 or any other Mini Shai-Hulud-listed scope (@antv, @lint-md, @openclaw-cn, @starmind, @cap-js, mbt). Step 2 — Contain: kill the bun and parent npm processes, network-isolate the host, snapshot disk and memory if forensics are in scope. Block bun.exe via WDAC/AppLocker on developer images that have no legitimate Bun use case. Step 3 — Hunt: query the package registry mirror or proxy for downloads of any Mini Shai-Hulud-listed package in the last 30 days across all dev hosts, and correlate against this UC to find every workstation that ran the loader. Rotate every credential the affected developer could touch.
// TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud: Bun spawned from npm preinstall
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "bun.exe" or FileName =~ "bun"
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe","npm-cli.js","node","npm","yarn","pnpm","npx"))
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("preinstall","setup.mjs","execution.js")
   or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath,
          InitiatingProcessParentFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
// TeamPCP Mini Shai-Hulud: Bun spawned from npm preinstall (Sentinel — SecurityEvent 4688 + ASIM)
union isfuzzy=true
(SecurityEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where EventID == 4688
  | where NewProcessName endswith "\\bun.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "/bun"
  | where (ParentProcessName has_any ("\\npm.exe","\\node.exe","\\yarn.exe","\\pnpm.exe","\\npx.exe","/npm","/node","/yarn","/pnpm","/npx"))
       or CommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js","preinstall")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account=SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source="SecurityEvent"),
(ImProcessCreate
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
  | where TargetProcessName endswith "bun.exe" or TargetProcessName endswith "/bun"
  | where (ParentProcessName has_any ("npm.exe","node.exe","yarn.exe","pnpm.exe","npx.exe"))
       or TargetProcessCommandLine has_any ("setup.mjs","execution.js")
       or ParentProcessCommandLine has "preinstall"
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer=DvcHostname, Account=ActorUsername, NewProcessName=TargetProcessName, CommandLine=TargetProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, Source="ImProcessCreate")
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Bun Runtime Spawned by npm Preinstall (Mini Shai-Hulud Loader)
